Hey @xaptronic, I wanted to give you a heads up that some recent changes that we made to session_state semantics (re-)introduced some strange behavior in the example script above that's reminiscent of the bug described in this issue. What happens now (as of version 0.89.0) is that the _second_ change to the widget is seemingly reverted after the user selects a new option.

Note that this is the behavior that was present pre-session state, and it's coming back now as we decided to make changes to our widget identity semantics so that they are consistent for keyed and unkeyed widgets (the session state changes made our widget identity semantics different for keyed vs unkeyed widgets, which caused a host of complications that we eventually decided would be best-resolved by returning to the old semantics). We now have a documentation page describing widget identity semantics [here](https://docs.streamlit.io/en/stable/advanced_widget_behavior.html).

The strange behavior with the radio button in this script resetting every second click is a consequence of the widget semantics we decided to adopt -- @AnOctopus described what's going on in more detail as well as provided a modified version of the script that achieves the desired behavior in https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/3827#issuecomment-924478275.

Hey, thanks for the video. I can immediately recognize this as partly caused by an issue that was brought up internally when reworking widgets, but I had opted to defer doing anything about because it seemed like a small edge case and I didn't want to jump into complicating things just before shipping. Multi-page apps are a much more compelling use case for other behaviors than I had been considering.

That issue is that setting the value of a widget through session state only applies during that script run, not following ones. It is possible to work around this by **passing a value stored in state as the default value argument for a widget**. The ability to access widget values through session state is in part to simplify the pattern of [set default value based on session state, update that session state value in the widget callback], but it only handles the simple case where a widget is rendered from the start.

The other issue is that widgets, including those that have values set through session state, do not have their state retained if they aren't rendered. You can similarly work around this by **keeping the widget values in a separate entry in session state and read from it to initialize the widget and write to it when the widget changes.** This is one of those behaviors that is exactly what some people expect and surprising for others, so improving it is tricky. We have wanted to do persistent widgets in some form since before session state, but it is a big task to make it come out just right so we haven't gotten to it yet (I spent a ton of time and effort on session state and it still has a number of edge cases and sources of confusion, so I expect persistent widgets to be similar).

This code worked in early versions of session state because widgets were persistent in a way that didn't play well with a lot of the widget implementations, which is why we changed them back to their transient behavior from before session state, but I wish we'd noticed the problem earlier so that we could have avoided breaking backwards compatibility.
So thanks for the response and help. I will work around it. I'm sure the re-write in 0.89 is only long-term positive for Streamlit. Great job getting to 1.0!

Hey @xaptronic -- I've been meaning to get back to you on some of the questions you asked, but I haven't been able to find the time in the past few weeks to do so until now. The team has been quite busy!

As to whether eventually tying widget state to query params will force you to change the way you currently do things, my hunch is that it won't (although I'm not able to give any true guarantees). Most likely, setting and reading most query params will work as it does currently, and we'll have a special namespace for the ones related to widget state.

To give a bit more insight into what's going on with these new widget identity semantics, the first thing to note is that they're technically not new semantics -- unkeyed widgets have (for as far back as I know) always had these semantics, and this is because in the unkeyed case, we don't have many other choices for what we use as the identity of a widget aside from (a hash of) the widget's arguments. I'm sure there are other ways of handling widget identity, but I'd imagine that each alternate approach has its own edge cases.

In the pre-session state world, keyed widgets similarly had their identities equal to a hash of the widget's arguments. This was something we wanted to change while implementing session state as some edge cases with widget behavior (specifically those where changing a widget's arguments "resets" the widget) could be solved by adding a key to widgets for which you wanted a more stable identity.

Unfortunately, we didn't quite understand all of the implications of doing this, and it turns out that more stable widget identities for keyed widgets ended up being quite problematic in cases where widget arguments can dynamically change. The most commonly appearing problem in this class of issues involved dynamically changing widget arguments invalidating the current value of a widget.

Another possible fix that would not require us to revert to the old keyed widget identity semantics involved handling the scenario where a widget value is invalidated by coercing the value to a sane default, but this seemed pretty messy and unsatisfactory given that how we choose a sensible default would have to be figured out on a case-by-case basis for all existing and future widgets.

The decision to revert back to the old semantics was essentially driven by the reasoning described above along with a growing sense of uncertainty around the decision to have inconsistent semantics for widget IDs in the keyed and unkeyed cases.

Hopefully this is helpful in explaining the rationale behind these decisions!

Hi @ryantaylor406, thanks for sharing that! The reason you're seeing this behavior is that when you change the value of the multiselect widget, the Streamlit app reruns (causing the value of the multiselect to revert to the value you had previously saved in session state). To avoid rerunning the app, you can use st.form to provide a submit button that users click after they've finished interacting with the multiselect widget. The app won't rerun until the user clicks that button. Here's an example (hosted [here](https://carolinedlu-debug-streamlit-app-4rnijd.streamlitapp.com/) so you can try it out):

Hey @treuille 

As of today, this is _expected behavior_, but I understand why this is confusing. We have adopted the mechanism that widgets that disappear from the page are removed from session state. There was a lot of confusion on what this means. The counter-bug we received is saying "Why does the widget continue to have a value after it disappeared?"

MPA demonstrates this problem by switching pages effectively removes widgets from session_state. There are two ways to think about the UX.

1.  MPA are "separate" apps. In this case, values set by session state are preserved, but values set by widget state (in session state) will disappear in the next run after the widget is removed. The idea is that each page is it's own self-functioning app, and therefore we expect the widget state to reset when going back to it.
2. MPA session state is all shared including widget state. This is what you are advocating as the expected behavior.

In the end, we identified (1) as the model to use and agreed on. I think the main reasoning is that to achieve (2) behavior, you simply save your widget state into session state as a separate variable. It's a little clunky though. I will leave this issue open to get feedback and ideas from the community.

Hi @kmcgrady,

Personally I've been aware of this for a long time and while I understand that this is a design decision, I have never understood the rationale for this particular choice.

One reason why I do not like it is that passing `key` to the widget is an explicit attempt to save the widget state in the session state. It is a very convenient syntactic sugar for associating widgets with explicit updates to `st.session_state` - or it would be, except it does not actually do that and it's not very upfront about that fact.

Personally, if the widget has been declared with the `key`, it usually means that I want to keep the state independently of whether the widget is currently displayed or not. Sometimes I do not care. And although I can certainly imagine valid reasons why someone would want the state to go away with the widget, I have never wanted it to, and if I did, I would prefer to explicitly clear the state anyway.

The fact that the saving is conditional on the widget being there and that fact is not very explicitly sign-posted in the description of the `key` parameter is very confusing to newcomers. I do not think it is much of an overstatement to say that on https://discuss.streamlit.io/ there is a thread about "why am I losing my widget state?" every other day.

For those of us who do know about it it results in code littered with callback functions which serve only the purpose of running the 'fake' widget session state into the 'real' persistent widget state.

I think the bottom line with this is that the way Streamlit state works now, there are three modes:

1. transient (normal widgets)
2. persistent (`st.session_state`)
3. persistent, but only sometimes (widget session state)

The existence of the third one is, in my opinion, not very useful.

Objectively, it is poorly documented. The [Session State API reference](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/api-reference/session-state) treats the two like as if they were the same thing:

>Every widget with a key is automatically added to Session State:

The [Multipage Apps](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/get-started/multipage-apps) site explicitly says:

>Pages share the same [st.session_state](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/session-state):

The linked page says:

1. Don't use keys. Instead, store the initial value inside the session state, and update the state manually.

2. If the widget goes out of view, make sure the initial values are up to date  

```python
from time import sleep
from streamlit.runtime.state import get_session_state
import streamlit as st

init_key = "__init_values__"


def main():
    view = st.radio("View", ["view1", "view2"])

    if view == "view1":
        text_input("Text1", key="text1")
        "☝️ Enter some text, then click on view2 above"
    elif view == "view2":
        "☝️ Now go back to view1 and see if your text is still there"

    st.write(st.session_state)


def text_input(label, key):
    if init_key not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state[init_key] = {}
    initial_values = st.session_state[init_key]
    try:
        value = initial_values[key]
    except KeyError:
        value = st.session_state.get(key, "")
        initial_values[key] = value

    value = st.text_input(label, value=value)

    st.session_state[key] = value
    return value


def ensure_hidden_widgets_loaded():
    new_session_state = get_session_state()._state._new_session_state
    for key, value in st.session_state.items():
        if key in new_session_state or key == init_key:
            continue
        st.session_state[init_key][key] = value


try:
    main()
finally:
    ensure_hidden_widgets_loaded()
```

What's likely going on here is that stopping the script run calls the internal method [ScriptRunner.request_stop](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/3626677888773768a82b44edd5092cbbcc0f2e6b/lib/streamlit/runtime/scriptrunner/script_runner.py#L190), which disconnects the session state to guard against a potential race condition where two `ScriptRunner`s are simultaneously mutating the same session state object. Your `asyncio` coroutines then try to access the `st.session_state` object and hit the `AttributeError`.

I think I'd consider this issue as falling somewhere on the border between a bug report and a feature request since our `ScriptRunner` infrastructure doesn't take into account ways that an app session's state can be asynchronously mutated by the user script. Support for this would probably require a good deal of work to reevaluate our assumptions around where async session state mutations can come from, and it's unlikely that we'd prioritize doing this without a significant increase in demand for supporting this from the community (I think these types of use-cases are relatively uncommon).

For now, I'd recommend the workaround (which is obvious enough that I'm sure you've already considered it) of having your coroutines exit early if expected session state keys disappear since that implies that the script has stopped.

This is an unfortunate consequence of how we handle the transience of widget state, and can't be fixed until we address widget persistence.

Streamlit used to work by always doing cleanup of "stale widgets" after a script run finished, even if it finished because it was interrupted. This would usually not be noticed because a rerun request would include the state of the widgets in the web app, even if they were just around because the active script run hadn't gotten to them yet. For fast reruns, we changed it so that interrupted runs wouldn't do the cleanup, though I can't recall exactly our reasoning for it and couldn't readily find it. We later made fast reruns the default.

That is the story for a single page app. For MPA, both [widgets on other pages persist] and [widgets on other pages reset] are perfect for some apps but would break others, and addressing it will be a big project, so we haven't done it yet. In the meantime, we get this awkward middle ground, where the persistence of widget state on another page depends on if the current page finished running before you switch back. We could try to fix it, but that would break other apps. A proper fix will require a notion of widget persistence.

In the meantime, as @vdonato notes, this behavior can be worked around by turning off fast reruns, though that will generally reduce responsiveness of script reruns.

@AnOctopus Did you or the team figure out yet what the long-term behavior of SessionState should be around page changes? 

I did some testing/logging of this too, I believe the behavior you describe is correct. 
When the user clicks on a page-change link, the frontend sends the re-run request to the backend and immediately clears its WidgetStateManager of inactive widgets (e.g. all of them, because the page is changing). However, the backend does not clear out old widget states until the active script_runner hits a "script finished" point. When this doesn't happen (because the user changed pages mid-run and fast-reruns are enabled), the old widget states are not removed.

There are two "root" issues going on:

### Issue 1: value-retention for widgets with user keys depends on previous script-runner finishing while active. 
This one is pretty easy to fix; but requires a choice.

> A. If the desire is to have user_key'd widgets retain their value across page changes the same way that custom user entries in `session_state` do, then the logic which cleans up widget states at the end of a script run needs to preserve those widgets' values -- it does not do so at present.

> B. If the desire is to have user_key'd widgets not retain their value across page changes, like widgets without a user_key, then ALL widget state needs to be cleared as soon as a re-run with a different page hash than the current one is requested.

### Issue 2: The desynchronization of WidgetStateManager (frontend) and SessionState (backend) when a page change occurs.
This is easy if you go with option B and commit to clearing ALL backend widget state every time a page changes. Nothing needs to get changed on the frontend because it's _already_ clearing it's widget state as soon as the page changes.

If you go with option A, then this is a lot tricker. Either, as you said above, the backend needs to send all the widget states it knows about to the front-end at the start of a re-run, OR the frontend WidgetStateManager needs to keep track of which widgets have a user_key, and purposefully avoid clearing those widgets' state when a page change is requested.

Streamlit isn't _really_ designed to be a "more user-friendly jupyter notebook", but here are some answers to your questions: 

> What is Streamlit's current recommended way to continuously save the session state so that if the session is randomly restarted, all is recovered. This has to be a fast process since again we often have large datasets in memory.

There isn't a "streamlit" way to do this -- you can handle it like you handle any other long-running python process: periodically save off a representation of your calculation "state" to disk and then program a means to load that state back into memory on application startup. One easy way to do this would be to periodically `pickle` the contents of `st.session_state`, although your mileage may vary depending on how "large" these large datasets you're talking about are. Large pandas datasets or numpy arrays have faster and more performant ways to be written to disk than the `pickle` library. You may also find it best to program in a way to detect which portions of the data have changed since the last save, and only save _those_ portions.

None of this is something that streamlit natively provides; so it will require you to write your own code for your own application.

> What is Streamlit's current recommended way to persist jobs being run by Streamlit instead of them getting killed if the session is restarted?

If the entire `streamlit` python process is getting killed and restarted:
* You need to run your long-running jobs as separate processes on the computer, and communicate with them via some means. What you're looking for is something like [Celery](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/getting-started/introduction.html), a python-based task scheduler that can be run along-side a streamlit-based UI. You can send it messages to have it start and stop certain jobs, and monitor their status as they run.

If it's just the user sessions that are getting removed and restarted (but the streamlit python process is persisting):
* You may be able to use something like my https://github.com/Asaurus1/streamlit-process-manager to spawn child python processes that will process your data and output results to a file that you can then read back into the streamlit front-end. Keep in mind, these library is in alpha so use it at your own risk.

You can make a class that contains all the state variables you need to access, and then a function that creates an instance of that class and returns it. If you decorate that function with cache_resource, That state object will be preserved across all sessions and available to every streamlit session.

It's obviously comes with all of the normal concurrency issues that you would get when you have multiple people accessing the same memory from different sessions. You could get around this by asking users to provide a username, and then giving them an instance of your new GlobalState class that is tied to their username. I'm doing the same, but with even more boilerplate as I'm using pydantic get validated, type safe session state. 

- I define one big session state Pydantic model 
- On every on_change / on_click etc. event I create a new copy of this object, replace the parameter, and sync it to the session state & query parameters. 

Here's an example with one widget / type:

```python
from typing import Literal

import streamlit as st
from pydantic import BaseModel


#####################
# Define basic types
#####################

Language = Literal["de", "en"]


class SelectedLanguage(BaseModel):
    value: Language


class ParameterSelection(BaseModel):
    selected_language: SelectedLanguage


# Type safe session state using a pydantic model
class SessionState(BaseModel):
    parameter_selection: ParameterSelection


######################################
# Typed session state setter / getter
######################################

def set_session_state(session_state: SessionState) -> None:
    """Set the session state. The session state is also added to the query
    parameters as a serialized JSON string. This allows the session state to
    be shared by simply sharing the URL."""
    st.session_state["session_state"] = session_state
    st.query_params["session_state"] = session_state.model_dump_json()


def get_session_state() -> SessionState:
    """Gets st.session state as a SessionState model. The session state
    is taken from the query parameters if present. If no session state is
    present at all it will be initialized with default values."""
    session_state = st.session_state.get("session_state")
    query_params = st.query_params.get("session_state")
    if query_params:
        try:
            session_state_from_query_params = SessionState.model_validate_json(
                query_params
            )
            return session_state_from_query_params
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Query parameters could not be deserialized: {e}")

    if not isinstance(session_state, SessionState):
        # Default / initial values are to be defined here
        # Each individual widget is responsible to deal with possible default
        # values that might not be valid, e.g. a language that's not in the
        # list of language as loaded from external data
        session_state = SessionState(
            parameter_selection=ParameterSelection(
                selected_language=SelectedLanguage(value="de"),
            )
        )

    return session_state

#################
# Define widgets
#################

def select_language() -> SelectedLanguage:
    WIDGET_KEY = "selected_language"

    def update_state() -> None:
        """Write widget state from st.session_state to typed session state
        pydantic model."""
        _current_session_state = get_session_state()
        _selected_language_validated = SelectedLanguage.model_validate(
            {"value": st.session_state.get(WIDGET_KEY)}
        )

        _updated_session_state = _current_session_state.model_copy()
        _updated_session_state.parameter_selection.selected_language = (
            _selected_language_validated
        )

        set_session_state(session_state=_updated_session_state)

    LANGUAGES = ["de", "en"]

    current_session_state = get_session_state()
    preselected_index = 0
    try:
        preselected_index = LANGUAGES.index(
            current_session_state.parameter_selection.selected_language.value
        )
    except ValueError:
        pass
    selected_language = st.selectbox(
        "Select a language:",
        LANGUAGES,
        preselected_index,
        key=WIDGET_KEY,
        on_change=update_state,
    )

    selected_language_validated = SelectedLanguage.model_validate(
        {"value": selected_language}
    )

    return selected_language_validated

##############
# Create page
##############

def page() -> None:
    select_language()

page()
```

Hi, I've found a way to combine threading & fragment to get a fairly responsive behavior. 

Note: the example below is just one way of using this technique; I have since moved to another more complicated variation, but this is the most straight forward one: (Thanks mainly to the SO answer, and what jcarroll showed me in another exchange.)

Hope the Streamlit team can package the 'run_in_thread' decorator up somehow.

```
import time
from functools import wraps
from threading import Thread

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

import streamlit as st
from streamlit.runtime.scriptrunner import add_script_run_ctx, get_script_run_ctx


## function wrapper
def run_in_thread(func):
    # per https://stackoverflow.com/questions/76472211/multithreading-for-streamlit-and-kite-connect
    @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        thread = Thread(target=func, args=args, kwargs=kwargs)
        ctx = get_script_run_ctx()
        add_script_run_ctx(thread, ctx)
        thread.start()
    return wrapper


# this is a fn that takes time to complete, (e.g. database call, etc.)
# so we run it in a thread
@run_in_thread
def generate_data(x=1, sleep=2):  # example from j.carroll
    print('in generate data fn')
    time.sleep(sleep)  # simulating the delay
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        np.random.randn(5, 5) * x, columns=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
    )
    print(f'returning df after sleep.. len={len(df)}')
    st.session_state.df = df


LOAD_FREQ = 10
@st.fragment(run_every=1)
def update_data():
    print('in update data fn')
    load_timer = st.session_state.load_timer
    now = time.monotonic()
    if now > load_timer + LOAD_FREQ:
        # avoid generating data all the time
        print('update data now > timer + freq')
        st.session_state.load_timer = now
        generate_data()


@st.fragment(run_every=1)
def filter_data(min_idx):
    print('in filter data fn')
    df = st.session_state.df
    st.session_state.df_f = df[df.index >= min_idx].copy()


@st.fragment(run_every=1)
def draw_graph(graph_slot):
    print('in draw graph fn')
    df = st.session_state.df_f
    if df is not None:
        graph_slot.plotly_chart(px.bar(df))


def init_states():
    if 'df' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.df = pd.DataFrame()
        st.session_state.df_f = pd.DataFrame()
    if 'load_timer' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.load_timer = time.monotonic()


def main():
    init_states()
    "`generate_data()` runs in the background, so these widgets remain fully interactive"
    st.button("Button 1")
    st.slider("Random slider", 0, 100)

    min_idx = st.selectbox('min idx', range(0, 5))
    graph_slot = st.empty()

    update_data()
    filter_data(min_idx)
    draw_graph(graph_slot)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

```

Having done a bunch of experimentation myself I have a few things to add.  There is a lot of inaccurate information floating around on the web about this subject.  The really important thing to remember is what's mentioned in the comment by @mescanne above:

> Every time a re-render is required (state change, user interaction, etc), a new thread is created and the script is run fresh. The old thread, if it hasn't already completed the script, may keep going (due to fastRerun) but any interaction with st objects will throw a Shutdown Exception.

This means that whlie you can use `asyncio.run()` in your script (the [Medium post](https://sehmi-conscious.medium.com/got-that-asyncio-feeling-f1a7c37cab8b) unfortunately linked from Streamlit's own documentation falsely claims otherwise), you can't allow any interaction with your app while the event loop is running, and any tasks you launch on it can't reliably access `st.` functions for the reasons mentioned above.  It will also lead to a possibly large number of threads being created since, as mentioned above, the resulting asyncio event loop may run forever.

While you can manually create an event loop, set it for the current thread, and recover it on future invocations of your script **in that same thread**, this isn't particularly useful because your script code may or may not (actually won't, probably) run on that thread.  You also can't, for example, call `run_until_complete` on the event loop for [well-known reasons](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/66435).

Also, despite what said Medium post claims, calling `asyncio.get_running_loop` **definitely does not** return Streamlit's own event loop, as it will always be on a different thread than the one that runs your script.  This is, of course, what this bug is actually about :-)  If you don't care about security, reliability, stability, etc, and you don't want to call `st.` functions from your tasks, you can get it by calling `_get_async_objs()` on the session runtime.  For instance:

```python
import asyncio
import time
import streamlit as st

loop = st.runtime.get_instance()._get_async_objs().eventloop

async def do_nothing(seconds):
    await asyncio.sleep(3)
    print("HELLO WORLD", seconds)

if st.button(label="Do something"):
    loop.create_task(do_nothing(time.time()))

if st.button(label="Do something else"):
    st.toast("Hello!")
```

The best workaround for the moment, if you need to use asyncio for something, is probably to explicitly create a separate thread to run asyncio tasks, using `add_script_run_ctx` to give it access to the session state so that it can communicate with the rest of the UI.

I also don't really see how a solution to this problem could easily be implemented in Streamlit.  Conceptually, what is necessary, is what the original poster's "ugly workaround" is supposed to do, and what the Medium post claims Streamlit does, but which neither of them actually do, namely creating (possibly on demand) an event loop for each session context which script code can use to launch tasks.  Why this doesn't work:

- Simply creating an event loop doesn't actually start it!  So calling `create_task` on said loop will not do anything at all.
- Running an event loop is a blocking, non-reentrant operation.   Obviously a Streamlit `AppContext` (which runs in the main thread) can't do this.   But also a Streamlit `ScriptRunner` (which runs in its own thread) can't do this either, because there could be any number of threads for a given session context.

I don't claim to really understand Streamlit's architecture but it seems like a possible implementation woud be to create a separate thread for each script context, run an event loop there, and somehow give script code access to this event loop so that it can create and wait on tasks launched in it.  The evil solution would be to do magic on `await` in script code to make it do that ;-)

- There is no signal handling possible in the local event loop.  So you have to hit Control-C multiple times to stop the server, and you will get an "Event loop is closed" exception.
- Any running tasks will do ... something undefined, I think ... if you stop the event loop, and Python will complain about this.

This is a frontend state synchronization bug in `st.selectbox` where the UI display becomes out of sync with the actual widget value. The issue occurs when a value is set programmatically via session state, and then the user opens and closes the dropdown without making a selection. The root cause appears to be in the shared Dropdown/Selectbox component (`frontend/lib/src/components/shared/Dropdown/Selectbox.tsx`), where the `valueBeforeRemoval` ref is only initialized once on mount and is not updated when the `propValue` changes via session state. When `handleBlur` fires, it may restore the stale initial value from this ref instead of the current value, causing the UI mismatch while the backend retains the correct value.

### Related Issues

- **#10093** - [In selectbox, if options change from None to not, the default value rendered is still None](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10093) - Similar UI state synchronization issue where the selectbox displays stale values when the underlying state changes. This is a confirmed bug with the same symptom of frontend/backend value mismatch.

This issue reports that when a WebSocket connection closes uncleanly (e.g., due to network disruptions), Streamlit creates a new session instead of reconnecting to the existing one, causing users to lose their session state.

**Root cause analysis:** The issue originates in `lib/streamlit/runtime/websocket_session_manager.py` in the `connect_session()` method. When a client attempts to reconnect with an existing session ID, the code checks if that session is already in `_active_session_info_by_id` (line 103). If it is, a warning is logged ("Session with id %s is already connected!") and a **new** session is created instead. The session can only be restored from storage if it's NOT currently active.

The core problem is a race condition: on an unclean WebSocket close, the server may not have detected the disconnect yet, so the session remains "active" in memory. When the client quickly reconnects with the same session ID, the server sees it as "already connected" and creates a new session instead of allowing reconnection. A potential fix would need to handle this case by either closing the existing connection first, implementing a grace period, or using a different strategy for tracking active vs. disconnected sessions.

Hey all — this issue has been on my radar and I wanted to share some design thinking. Sharing it here since this issue already captures the problem well and I'd love to get reactions.

### The idea: `st.background_task`

A managed API for kicking off long-running work that survives reruns:

```python
task = st.background_task(slow_query, args=(params,), key="my_query")

if task.running:
    st.info("Query running...")
elif task.done:
    st.dataframe(task.result)
```

The `key` deduplicates across reruns (same key = same task, not a new one). When the task finishes, the runtime automatically triggers a rerun so you can render the result — no polling needed. Tasks get cleaned up when the session ends.

The workaround @mkleinbort-ic shared above with raw threads works, but threads created outside Streamlit don't have access to `ScriptRunContext`, can't trigger reruns on completion, and aren't tied to the session lifecycle. This would handle all of that.

### How it relates to parallel fragments

We're working on `@st.fragment(parallel=True)` ([#14277](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14277)) which gives concurrency *within* a single script run — independent UI sections load at the same time. Background tasks would be different: the work outlives reruns, produces data rather than UI, and doesn't block interactions. They'd be complementary.

### Open questions

- Does the API shape feel right? The original proposal here used a decorator (`@st.run_in_background`) — any preference?
- What are your actual use cases? Long queries, model training, batch jobs?
- How important is cancellation when inputs change?

Would love to hear what people think.

This is a **bug / upstream-dependency regression**. Streamlit's `lib/pyproject.toml` currently declares `websockets>=12.0.0,<17`, which still allows `websockets` to resolve to **16.1** (released 2026-07-09). This is a confirmed **regression** (works in `1.58.0`, crashes in every version from `1.59.0` onward). When a fragment calls `.status()` on a container declared *outside* the fragment and then opens that status block with two separate `with` statements, the app crashes to a blank page with `Uncaught Error: Cannot set a node at a delta path`.

**Root cause** (matches the reporter's excellent analysis): `StatusContainer._create` captures the delta path from the **parent cursor before** the block is created (`lib/streamlit/elements/lib/mutable_status_container.py:81-91`). Since `1.59.0`, a write from a fragment into an outside container is redirected into a per-fragment layout-transparent wrapper block, so the status (`expandable`) block actually lands one level deeper than the captured path predicted. The stale `_delta_path` therefore points at the `transparent` wrapper instead of the status. On the second `with`, `__exit__` calls `update(state="complete")`, which re-emits the status block directly at that stale path (`mutable_status_container.py:151`). On the frontend, `AppRoot.addBlock` only inherits the existing children when the block type matches (`frontend/lib/src/render-tree/AppRoot.ts:467-483`); `transparent` ≠ `expandable`, so the whole subtree is dropped and the next element is written to a path whose parent no longer exists, causing `SetNodeByDeltaPathVisitor` to throw. Note the one-`with` variant silently corrupts the tree without a visible crash.

A promising fix is to capture `_delta_path` **after** `_block()` from the path it actually wrote to, rather than predicting it from the parent cursor beforehand; other elements that store a delta path and later enqueue a message with it directly should be audited too.

### Triage summary

This is a **dependency-compatibility bug** in Streamlit's web server, not a Community Cloud–specific problem — it affects any environment where a fresh install resolves Starlette to a newer release (Community Cloud just happens to auto-resolve the latest compatible versions).

**Root cause:** Streamlit's custom gzip middleware (`lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_gzip_middleware.py`) subclasses and directly instantiates Starlette's *internal* `GZipResponder`/`IdentityResponder` classes, which are private implementation details rather than public API:

```python
responder = _MediaAwareGZipResponder(
    self.app, self.minimum_size, compresslevel=self.compresslevel
)
```

`_MediaAwareGZipResponder` does not override `__init__`, so it inherits Starlette's constructor. A newer Starlette release changed `GZipResponder.__init__` to add a required keyword-only argument `thread_minimum_size`. Because the responder is instantiated without it, startup fails before any app code runs:

```
TypeError: GZipResponder.__init__() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'thread_minimum_size'
```

Streamlit's runtime dependency range in `lib/pyproject.toml` is `starlette>=0.46.0,<2`, so the incompatible Starlette version satisfies the upper bound (`<2`) and gets installed. This coupling to Starlette internals was introduced with the Starlette/Uvicorn server migration ([#14553](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14553)).

**Workaround confirmed by multiple reporters:** pin `starlette<1.4.0` (e.g. `starlette==1.3.1`) in `requirements.txt`.

**Suggested fix:** cap the Starlette upper bound below the breaking release (and/or make the middleware resilient to the changed responder signature, e.g. forward `thread_minimum_size` or stop relying on the private responder classes).

### Related Issues

- [#15378 – Running Streamlit with Starlette in Corporate Network](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15378): Another `area:server` bug stemming from the Starlette/Uvicorn migration; related to server behavior introduced by the same migration, though a different symptom (WebSocket connectivity).
- [#15022 – Intermittent `OSError: [WinError 121]` since upgrading to `v1.57.0`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15022): Also traces back to the 1.57 Starlette/Uvicorn migration and touches the same server layer, indicating shared risk in the new Starlette stack.

No existing issue appears to be a duplicate of this specific `GZipResponder`/Starlette-version incompatibility.

This is a real Components V2 race, not identity churn and almost certainly not `_pending_resets`. With an explicit `key`, the element id stays stable (`key_as_main_identity=True`), but `useHandleJsContent` still re-runs the default export whenever `data` changes. A mount-time `setTriggerValue` then has to win a one-shot delivery race: the value is stored under the synthetic trigger-aggregator id (`$$STREAMLIT_INTERNAL_KEY_<id>__events`), flushed on `setTimeout(0)`, deleted from client widget state, and cleared again by `_reset_triggers()` at the end of every script run.

That aggregator id is not in the render tree, so `removeInactiveWidgetState()` on `ScriptFinished` can delete a pending trigger before the macrotask flush sends it. `_coalesce_widget_states` also preserves `trigger_value` / `chat_input_value` across queued reruns but not `json_trigger_value`, so a second widget-update message can overwrite a just-queued CCv2 trigger. Both fit the controls: `setStateValue` lives on the element id and persists; event-handler triggers fire after the app has settled. `_pending_resets` is page-scope persist-state tracking and is not involved in this repro.

A browser session keeps the value, and `persist_state="session"` keeps it in `AppTest`. `AppTest._run()` builds a new `PagesManager` on every run, and that manager's current page hash starts as `""`. `ScriptRunner` compares that empty hash with the target page (the main-script hash when no page was requested), treats the rerun as a page change, and runs page-change widget cleanup before `ScriptRunContext.reset()` installs the real page hash. Page-scoped persistence then sees a different page and drops the preserved value, including the pending reset that makes the remounted widget ignore its stored value. A contributor reproduced this on `develop`; seeding the new manager with the requested hash stops the false page change, but that also makes the current and requested hashes identical after `switch_page()`, so the pre-run cleanup that should drop page-scoped state before the new page registers widgets would be skipped. The seed needs to be the page from the previous run, with the requested hash passed separately.

Thanks for the report, @joemaish2b<https://github.com/joemaish2b>. I can reproduce this on Streamlit 1.64.0 with the same error message. The code that causes it is unchanged in 1.65.0 and on develop, so upgrading will not fix it yet. After the error, the page stops updating until you reload it.

Workaround: create .streamlit/config.toml in the folder where you run streamlit run, add these lines, and restart the app:

[global]
minCachedMessageSize = 1e12

This turns off the message cache where the error happens. In my tests the app had 0 errors in about 800 clicks with this setting, and failed in 3 of 3 runs without it. The cost is network traffic: Streamlit sends large elements, such as big dataframes, to the browser in full on every rerun.

I could only trigger the error by clicking a button or moving a slider while the app was rerunning. Refresh loops with nobody clicking ran about 2,300 times without an error. So two questions:

  1.  Do people click or change widgets on the page while it refreshes? Or does the error also appear when nobody touches the page?
  2.  How does your app refresh every second? For example st.fragment(run_every=1), st_autorefresh, or time.sleep(1) followed by st.rerun().
